content.summary_of_the_paper: The authors focus on a special setting in meta-learning, where explicit metadata about tasks that could provide useful context for task adaptation is readily available. They investigate conditioning models with this task metadata to improve model performance. Second, they propose a simple method to prevent memorization of certain tasks negatively affecting performance based on the explicit task metadata available in their setting. The authors evaluate their work on a geospatial and remote sensing dataset with applications to agricultural policy making, for which metadata is prevalent, but that suffers from limited labelled data and data imbalance. They also evaluate on Omniglot dataset to demonstrate general applicability of the method.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
The paper is clearly written and results are strong. While only applicable to certain settings with readily available task-metadata, the paper convinces that separate consideration of this settings is a good idea.

There are a few weaknesses:

- While ablation performed by the authors shows the importance of forgetfulness and while the thresholds triggering forgetfulness are documented in A.1, it remains unclear how often forgetfulness is actually triggered during training on the different tasks. 

- The authors do not back up their claim that the Grouped-Omniglot task "is a much more challenging setup than the typical setup of mixing all characters together, since more similar characters will need to be differentiated". While this claim is verifiable by looking up performance of comparable baselines on the original Omniglot task, this information should be included in the paper. 

- The authors compare against a "pre-training baseline" trained to "classify all data as crop or non-crop (without task metadata), then fine-tuned on the test task training data". While a valid task, the term "pre-training" here is misleading as pre-training typically refers to a large scale, unsupervised learning stage. Arguably large-scale pretraining on unlabeled geo-spatial and remote-sensing data may render authors proposed metadata conditioning less helpful. The authors method is certainly more data and computationally efficient (being trained on a single K80 GPU). Future comparisons against large-scale geo-spatial pretraining will be interesting.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The paper is clearly written and introduces a novel idea. Experiments are thorough and convincing. The paper includes details on the experiments and the authors promise to publish the code and all models. The proposed method is also computationally accessible (Single K-80 GPU for the CNN models), helping with reproducibility.
content.summary_of_the_review: The introduced task-informed meta-learning for conditioning meta-learning models with explicit task metadata helps advance the state of the art in the important domain of crop classification and agricultural yield estimation, a impactful task with relations to agricultural policy and climate change. The authors propose two simple ideas and demonstrate that they have significant positive impact on model performance.
content.correctness: 3: Some of the paper’s claims have minor issues. A few statements are not well-supported, or require small changes to be made correct.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 3: The contributions are significant and somewhat new. Aspects of the contributions exist in prior work.
content.empirical_novelty_and_significance: 3: The contributions are significant and somewhat new. Aspects of the contributions exist in prior work.

content.title: Response to reviewer V1DY
content.comment:
Thank you for your time and thoughtful comments. We address specific points of your review below:

1. “ *it remains unclear how often forgetfulness is actually triggered during training on the different tasks.* ” Thank you for pointing this out. We have added this information to the appendix (Table 4). 

2. “ *While this claim is verifiable by looking up performance of comparable baselines on the original Omniglot task, this information should be included in the paper.* ” We updated section 5.3. to better draw attention to this.

3. “ *While a valid task, the term "pre-training" here is misleading as pre-training typically refers to a large scale, unsupervised learning stage. Arguably large-scale pretraining on unlabeled geo-spatial and remote-sensing data may render authors proposed metadata conditioning less helpful.* ” While we agree that large-scale unsupervised pre-training would be a powerful baseline, there have not been any widely used large-scale pretraining methods applied to earth observation data (especially time-series earth observation data, which is a particular focus of this work). In addition, much recent few-shot learning in earth observation contexts has focussed on meta-learning [1, 2, 3], motivating the investigation of meta-learning in this work.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper studies the problem of meta learning with explicit task information. Compared to other meta-learning based methods, this paper proposed an algorithm named Task-Informed Meta-Learning (TIML) that extends the MAML algorithm by using task explicit information. More specifically, the proposed algorithm included a task encoder that generates two vectors for each weight in the model to do a feature-wise linear modulation. It also introduces a simple mechanism to discard training of a task that performs better than a performance threshold to prevent ‘memorization’. Experimental results on crop type prediction, crop yield estimation and Omniglot dataset suggest the proposed TIML method outperforms other baselines.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths
- This paper studies a very meaningful problem of meta-learning with task information. 
- The proposed framework seems to be reasonable and perform well on benchmark datasets.
- The proposed method is simple and efficient to leverage the task information.

Weaknesses
- Technical novelty. I feel the technicality of the proposed method is relatively limited. (1) the use of task information itself is not novel, existing work in MAML can be easily extended to use task information. (The novelty of this paper in my understanding is to use task encoder to leverage task information). (2) The ‘forgetfulness’ idea seems to be quite straight-forward and lacks a more theoretical understanding. Is there any existing work that discusses ‘memorization’ in a similar way, and whether the proposed method can achieve some guaranteed generalization performance? 

- Presentation and clarity. The presentation of this paper can be improved. For example, there are some unclear notions being used in the paper that need to be clarified, such as f_{\theta_m} in algorithm 1. 

- Experiment section can be improved. One main contribution of this paper is the introduction of the task encoder, therefore, I think more experiments on ablating the task encoder is needed. For example, can we directly feed task information to all baseline methods (similar to the No encoder setup)? And can we make task embedding just addictive or concatenate to the hidden layers (to test the usefulness of FiLM)?
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: This paper’s presentation and clarity can be improved. The proposed method is simple and efficient, but may lack novelty or justification. The code/dataset on conducting the experiments is open-sourced.
content.summary_of_the_review: This paper proposed TIML, a meta-learning algorithm that makes use of explicit task information. Overall the proposed algorithm is simple and efficient and archives good results on multiple benchmark datasets. However, I think the novelty of the proposed algorithm is limited. This can be improved by providing more justification and insights on the design of task encoder and ‘forgetfulness’ and an improved experiment section.

content.title: Response to reviewer 1Xim
content.comment:
Thank you for your time and thoughtful comments. 

You stated concerns around the novelty of this work (“*the use of task information itself is not novel*”). While the incorporation of task information into the meta-learning process may seem clear in retrospect, previous methods *have not included the metadata in the learning process at all*. Previous approaches have attempted to infer clusters of tasks without supervision, but, surprisingly no approaches have leveraged available task metadata in any way [1, 2]. 

Even in geospatial meta learning, where the location metadata is inherently available, this information has not been leveraged. For example, previous works investigating the highly societally impactful task of crop classification [3, 4, 5] have not made use of location (or any other task) information. We therefore view our contribution as **both** the inclusion of task information in the meta-learning process, and the specific architecture (TIML) used to achieve this. **Considering the magnitude of our improvement over such previous works, our innovation is highly meaningful**.

You asked if we can “feed task information to all baseline methods (similar to the No encoder setup)?”. In addition to the "No encoder" setup, the Deep Gaussian Process baseline for the yield estimation task receives the task information as input as well. **Our method outperforms both the "no encoder" ablation and the Deep Gaussian Process model**. 

We also note that passing task information to all baselines - as you requested - **is not possible (or useful) due to differences in the semantic resolution of the data**. For example, if we passed task information to the randomly initialised model - which only sees a single task - the task information values would be constant for all the datapoints seen by the model, so it would not be helpful in discriminating positive and negative examples. 

Finally, you asked about “*existing work discussing memorization*”. [6] investigated  over-performance (‘memorization’) on common or easy tasks in meta-learning settings, and [7,8,9] are also prior attempts at handling this. We emphasise the simplicity of our method compared to these prior approaches, especially considering the improvement in performance it yields.

Thank you for highlighting issues in our presentation and clarity. We have updated our description of $\theta_m$. Is there anything else we can clarify?

Weaknesses

It should be very trivial to use those metadata as additional inputs to the meta-learner and extend the existing meta-learning methods to incorporate them. I encourage the authors to clarify this.

content.title: Response to reviewer htYF
content.comment:
Thank you for your time and thoughtful comments.

We **do compare against baselines that have access to the task metadata**. Specifically, (i) in the crop classification task, we compare against a version of MAML where the task inputs are “appended to every raw input timestep and passed directly to the classifier”, and (ii) in the yield estimation task we compare against a Deep Gaussian Process baseline which also has access to the task data. **In both cases, our method significantly outperforms these methods**.

In addition, you stated that incorporating metadata into the learning process is trivial. In fact, there is significant active research exploring how metadata can inform learning (outside the context of meta-learning). The “Learning from metadata” paragraph in our Related Works section cites works published in (among other conferences) ICLR 2020 [1] and additional examples.

Finally, you commented that you “*don't understand why the metadata should be seen as something external or something invisible to other meta-learning methods*”. While incorporating task information into the meta-learning process may seem clear in retrospect, **previous methods have not included the metadata in the learning process at all**. This is all the more significant considering there are “*tons of papers regarding task-adaptive meta-learning*” as you described. Clearly, **given the number of past works on such problems, and the magnitude of our improvement over such works, our innovation is highly meaningful**.

More specifically, previous approaches have attempted to infer clusters of tasks without supervision, but surprisingly no approaches have leveraged available task metadata in any way [5, 6]. Even in geospatial meta learning, where the location metadata is inherently available, previous works [2, 3, 4] have not made use of this information - these works did not even pass in metadata as an auxiliary input (which as we noted above is an approach that is significantly outperformed by TIML).

content.title: Response to authors
content.comment:
Thanks for clarifying that the authors have already compared to the baselines that incorporates the task metadata. After the internal discussion with AC and other reviewers, I decided to increase my score to 3.

One of the reviewers mentioned that the datasets and settings the authors used is somewhat new and of particular importance. I'm not sure those aspects are well aligned with this type of conference. My evaluation is mainly based on the machine learning aspects of the problem and methodology.

Also, even if the previous meta-learning methods have not considered task meta-data as an input, this is precisely because this problem formulation is essentially not different from conditioning on only a support set. As reviewer 1sSR mentioned, any meta-learner can do this without significant modification in their architectures. The proposed method is one of them (a simple modification of MAML). It means that as well as the technical novelty, the problem formulation itself seems quite trivial to address.

Sincerely,
Reviewer htYF

content.title: Response to Reviewer htYF
content.comment:
Thank you for your response.

It is not correct that this problem formulation is “essentially not different from conditioning on the support set”. Indeed, **we benchmark against and significantly outperform this formulation**. Specifically, we significantly outperform the MMAML benchmarks (which conditions on the support set) in the crop-classification and grouped omniglot tasks.

The ICLR Call for Papers explicitly calls for applications in “climate, sustainability”. The CropHarvest dataset (which we use for the crop classification task) was published at NeurIPS by NASA; we strongly feel that the demonstrated impact of the paper on high-profile sustainability-related tasks is an active positive, rather than somehow disqualifying our paper from consideration at ICLR. 

Finally, our method yields **significant performance improvements over MAML**, and succeeds where MAML fails entirely (on the yield estimation task). Therefore, our algorithmic innovation is clearly not trivial, since MAML has been investigated extensively and these significant gains have been missed in all the prior literature.

content.title: Response to reviewer 1sSR
content.comment:
Thank you for your time and thoughtful comments.

You stated that we use “*exactly the same method as MMAML*”. Our method is significantly different from MMAML. In fact, we use MMAML as a baseline, and significantly outperform it (see Table 1, Figure 1, Table 3).

The key difference in our method is the **explicit use of task metadata** to inform task adaptation. Using task metadata has not been explored before. Previous approaches have attempted to infer clusters of tasks, but surprisingly no approaches have leveraged available metadata on tasks [1, 2]. We show in our paper that (i) metadata can be extremely helpful in improving generalization with limited data and (ii) our TIML method performs significantly better than the naive approach of simply including metadata as part of the input to the model.

You stated that “*every meta-learning application papers use the meta-data*.” We have not found this to be the case. In addition to the examples above, we highlight the specific example of meta-learning in geospatial contexts, where location data is inherently available. Despite plentiful previous research [2, 3, 4] no previous works have made use of location (or any other) meta-data as input when training the model.

Finally, we are solving two highly impactful tasks (crop classification and yield estimation) using real data provided to NASA in order to help address food insecurity. These are label-constrained tasks (published at NeurIPS and AAAI) which previous research has attempted to solve using few-shot learning approaches. **Our method significantly improves on the results of this previous research.**
